comment.value:
This paper introduces a novel, learning-based approach to generating simpler Craig interpolants for Linear Integer Arithmetic (LIA), a crucial component in formal verification. The proposed method uses a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to guide SMT solvers like Z3, and demonstrates a significant reduction in the complexity of the generated interpolants on a new, large-scale dataset created by the authors.

The reviewers are split. There is consensus on the novelty and originality of the work. However, there are significant disagreements, importantly along the axis of future significance and generalization. 

I am leaning to accept the paper on the basis of starting a new, hopefully fruitfull, interaction between ML and symblic methods.

With the discussion period almost over, we would like to make a few final remarks. 

Although much of this thread has focused solely on downstream applications, we hope the other key contributions of our work are not overlooked — including the design of our encodings and networks, their novel integration with symbolic methods, and the introduction of the first scalable dataset for this problem. 

We thank all reviewers for their assessments and responses.

Below we provide an analysis of the solutions. For each problem, the interpolation query was created by unfolding the transition relation twice. Formula A thus describes states that are reachable in at most two loops from the initial states, and formula B describes states that are reachable to error states in at most two loops. A problem is solved if an inductive invariant is found.

Among the 10 problems we tested, 5 were solved by both the original Z3 and guided Z3. The rest were not solved by either of them.

Among the 5 solved ones (#9, #10, #17, #25, #30)
- For 4 of them, both provided the same solutions, with the complexity averaging at 1.
- For 1 problem, the original Z3’s solution has complexity 3, and the guided version’s solution has complexity 1. 
  + #17. Original Z3 solution: ( x < 2 || m < n )  && ( m < 2 || m < n)  
  + #17. Guided Z3 solution: ( m < 2 || m < n). 

Among the 5 unsolved ones (#1, #3, #15, #23, #24)
- For all of them, both provided the same solutions that are not inductive invariants, with complexity 0 (i.e., a single LIA formula without connectives).

**Takeaways**: The results on XC correspond to our earlier comments that XC problems are relatively easy and do not benefit much from a better interpolantion solver. That said, the reduction in time is still significant and valuable in practice because of the repeated invocation of the process.

The unsolved instances are likely due to the naive handcrafting approach used here, which can be viewed as a bare-bones version of a modern solver. More sophisticated approaches in practice would combine interpolants with predicate abstraction or property-directed reachability (PDR) to boost the success rate.

We hope this demonstrates our commitment to addressing the concerns raised by the reviewers.

title.value: Preliminary results on reduced solver time

comment.value:
We have conducted the suggested experiment by manually deducing interpolation
queries from 10 sampled problems in XC. For each problem, the interpolation
query was created by unfolding the transition relation twice. We then ask both
the original Z3 and Z3 guided by the model (without retraining on XC) to give solutions.

Below we first report the preliminary results on the average solving time.

| Method | Solver Time (s) | Delta |
|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| Original Z3 | 0.014 | - |
| Guided Z3 | 0.010 | -28.6% |

The time reduction here is consistently observed for every problem. This is by itself already beneficial because interpolation queries are made repeatedly when solving a whole verification problem. 

Later we will follow up with a more detailed analysis on the solutions.

---

We would also like to apologize if any of our comments came across as confrontational to any of the reviewers — **that was never our intention**. We sometimes raise questions, and we genuinely value the answers and the opportunity for dialogue. We believe that identifying and discussing misunderstandings in a respectful manner is a healthy and essential part of the review process.

>  If time is a constraint, a sample of 10 problems...

By time constraints we are not concerned about the time for experiments (including conversion of benchmark problems) but about the time for engineering efforts to perform meaningful integration into modern verification tools (which are known for their complexity), as reviewer eKSy pointed out in the previous comments in this thread.

> Is it possible to use Z3 as the solver (I believe Spacer is the underlying CHC engine)?

We couldn’t quite follow the suggestions here and would appreciate further elaboration from the reviewer.

Z3 provides various features: an ordinary SMT solver, an interpolating prover, and a CHC solver (a.k.a Spacer).

Our understanding is that Spacer uses model-based projection rather than the interpolation solver of Z3. So, running Spacer for solving Inv_Track benchmark does not help evaluate our interpolation model.

Could you please clarify what exactly you mean here?

---

**But then the reviewers may ask: where is the claimed interpolation usage in modern solvers?**

Predicate abstraction-based tools like Eldarica [1] and MoCHi [2] use interpolants, but the integration into them needs the support for other theories and possibly also generalization to “tree interpolants”. This is why we have been emphasizing the necessity of handling combinations of theories.

We hope this helped clarify concerns on the applications further.

---

[1] *The ELDARICA Horn Solver,*, H. Hojjat and P. Rümmer, 2018 Formal Methods in Computer Aided Design (FMCAD), Austin, TX, USA, 2018, pp. 1-7, doi: 10.23919/FMCAD.2018.8603013.

[2] *Predicate abstraction and CEGAR for higher-order model checking*, Kobayashi, Naoki and Sato, Ryosuke and Unno, Hiroshi, PLDI 2011, ACM SIGPLAN Notices, Volume 46, Issue 6, Pages 222 - 233

Thank you for your follow-up and thoughtful questions!
>  "I appreciate you running the CVC5 comparison as well and would recommend this be added to the appendix of the manuscript."

**Response**: Thank you! We will definitely add this extra experiment to the appendix.

> What [are] the confidence interval of the Z3 times and cvc5 times?

**Response:** We agree with your observation that the 66% reduction reported for CVC5 might reflect the smaller number of problems it successfully solves. Below we provide the 95% confidence intervals for mean solving times. Even under conservative estimation, the time reduction for CVC5 remains around ~28%, which is comparable to the ~30% reduction observed for Z3:
- CI for the Z3 (guided) mean: (0.00887, 0.00995)
- CI for the Z3 (original) mean: (0.01181, 0.01283)
- CI for the CVC5 (guided) mean: (0.07628, 0.13735)
- CI for the CVC5 (original) mean: (0.18424, 0.41703)

> What is the input format ? Would SV-COMP or sygus loop invariant benchmarks be potentially runnable?

**Response:** Our implementation accepts primarily natural infix notation(e.g., $x + y \le 4 \wedge x \ge 2$) and partially SMT-LIB2.

However, evaluating on downstream SV-COMP or SyGuS Inv_Track benchmark would require significantly more engineering effort. As we noted in our response to reviewer eKSy, a fundamental challenge arises from the combination of theories. Downstream solvers or tasks (e.g., SV-COMP) often require reasoning across multiple theories — for example, combining LIA with array theory, Boolean theory (referring to variables ranging in Booleans in addition to integers) or equality reasoning (possibly between formulas).

Adapting our system to such settings would require not only new parsers, typing infrastructure, and encodings, but also the **design of sound and complete mathematical schemes or tricks** for computing interpolants separately for each theory and then combining them. This is particularly necessary because we want the LIA segment to be handled by the model. These challenges — both theoretical and engineering — go beyond the scope of the current work.

(The “XC” category of SyGuS 2019 Inv_Track requires only integers, but most of them are now easily solvable with existing CHC solvers, so they would not benefit much from a better interpolation subroutine in terms of solvability.)

---

We hope the reviewers will recognize these limitations as intrinsic to the problem setting and take them into account during final assessment.

Thank you again for the constructive feedback!

Thank you for the review. We understand that unfamiliarity with the field may have led to some confusion, and we would like to clarify each of the concerns raised.

> “It's unclear to what extent one can verify the claim of "simplicity" compared to previous solutions, the definition of simplicity was not made clear.” & “... the complexity of the interpolants it produces can be reduced by up to 47.3%. Not sure how this figure was reached”

We respectfully clarify the reviewer’s concern regarding the notion of “simplicity” and how the reported 47.3% reduction was measured.

We define the complexity of a formula as the number of logical connectives it contains—specifically, the number of $\wedge$ and $\vee$ operators. This **definition is formally stated on lines 62–63 in Section 2** and aligns with the standard interpretation of formula complexity in the verification literature.

The term “simplicity” is thus used in a precise and quantitative sense. All comparisons in Table 2 and Table 3 follow this definition. Specifically, the 47.3% reduction figure is derived from Table 2:

- Average complexity of Z3’s original interpolants: 5.38

- Average complexity of model-guided interpolants: 2.83

- Percentage reduction: (5.38−2.83)/5.38×100%=47.3%

> “It would help me to understand exactly where and how interpolants are used and why the problem of producing "simpler" interpolants is important as well as a better explanation of the "simplicity" definition.”

We explain this as a common response to reviewers gZmf, eKSy and DWpJ as follows.

---

# Addressing the Concern on Potential Impact
We noticed that the only substantive concern raised by reviewers eKSy and gZmf centers on the potential impact of our work. Reviewer DWpJ echoed this by asking “Why is producing simpler interpolants important?”

This is an oversight on our part. While we briefly mentioned the reasons on lines 19–21, we did not elaborate further, as this fact is often taken for granted in the literature on interpolation-based verification.

We now provide a clarification on the significant impact of simpler interpolants, addressing both conceptual and practical aspects. 

We would like to emphasize that this is not an artificial problem chosen merely to showcase machine learning techniques. Rather, it addresses a longstanding and practical challenge in formal verification—one that directly impacts the effectiveness and scalability of verification tools.

## Conceptually

In program verification, Craig interpolants are often used to extract candidate invariants from proofs of bounded cases. Intuitively, an interpolant is a formula that captures a property implied by one part of the system and inconsistent with another, using only the common variables.

**The key insight is that simplicity leads to generality.** A simpler interpolant tends to omit the incidental details of a particular execution, making it more likely to hold in general (i.e. be inductive for all executions).

This is analogous to machine learning, where a simple model that captures the core pattern will generalize better than an overly complex one that overfits to training data. In the verification context, a complex interpolant can “overfit” a bounded proof (including many specific corner-case conditions), whereas a concise interpolant focuses on the essential relationship and is less prone to depend on particular aspects of that bounded run.

The result is an interpolant that is more likely to be a true invariant for the unbounded system, rather than a brittle formula that breaks with minor changes. A concise interpolant (e.g. a single linear inequality or equality) is less tied to a specific execution, so it generalizes to new executions. Invariant generation becomes easier because the formula isn’t cluttered with special-case conditions that might fail as soon as we go beyond the originally analyzed trace.

In short, simpler interpolants serve as more general and robust invariants, which is exactly what we need for scalable verification.

### **Example**:

Consider the following example of finding a loop invariant. Suppose we have a C program:
```
x = 0; y = 0;
while(*) {x++; y+=2}
assert(x=100=> y=200);
```
The key to proving the assertion lies in discovering the loop invariant y = 2x. A common strategy for finding such invariants is interpolation. 

Let $I(x,y)$ be an (unknown) invariant.

Then by unfolding the loop a few times, we would get the constraints:

$(x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4) \Rightarrow I(x,y)$

$I(x,y) \Rightarrow (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

This induces the interpolation problem:

$A = (x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4)$

$B = \neg (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

All of

$I_1 = (x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4)$

$I_2 = (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

$I = y = 2x$

are interpolants between A and B, but only $y=2x$, the simplest among these, is a valid loop invariant of the original C program.

### **Where is the difficulty?**
In practice, interpolation solvers can (and often) generate interpolants like $I_1$ or $I_2$. In the simple two dimensional case as in this example, a human expert might be able to simplify the solutions by hand. But it quickly becomes infeasible in higher dimensions (i.e., more variables) with more regions (i.e., more logic connectives). 

Whether machine learning can guide interpolation solvers to find simpler interpolants automatically has been an open question. Our work makes the first attempt to guide interpolation solvers toward producing simpler interpolants, and shows that this is both possible and effective.

## Practically
From an engineering perspective, using simpler interpolants pays off in the following ways.

- **Verification Convergence**: Interpolants are used iteratively to search for an inductive invariant. Simpler interpolants are more likely to generalize across all program executions, increasing the probability that one of them will be inductive. This, in turn, improves the chance that the verification process will eventually succeed. In contrast, overly complex interpolants tend to overfit bounded traces and often fail to generalize, which can cause the verification loop to stagnate or diverge entirely. As a result, the system may perform many unproductive solver calls or even time out.

- **Solver efficiency**: Less complex formulas are cheaper for solvers to handle. Every additional literal or clause in an interpolant is something the downstream SMT query has to reason about. A 447-clause interpolant might trigger many more internal computations (Boolean case splits, calls to arithmetic subsolvers, etc.) than a 2-clause interpolant. By keeping interpolants minimal, we cut down the search space and the overhead in the subsequent SAT/SMT procedures. This often translates to more solvable downstream problems and/or faster verification times, as seen in Figure 4 of [1].

- **Proof reuse**: Simpler interpolants often enable a more compositional verification approach, where one can reuse the same inductive argument across different components or unrolling lengths. If the invariant is a small conjunction of facts, it can be plugged in modularly; if it’s a huge disjunction of special cases, it’s much harder to reuse or even comprehend. Thus simplicity can improve the scalability of the verification process itself, not just the single SMT query.

For further theoretical justification and more empirical evidence, we refer to the classical literature by Aws Albarghouthi and Kenneth L. McMillan such as [1].

[1] *Beautiful Interpolants.* Aws Albarghouthi and Kenneth L. McMillan. CAV 2013: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Computer Aided Verification - Volume 8044 Pages 313 - 329

---

We hope these clarify the confusion! We would greatly appreciate it if you could take our response into account when considering the final score.

Thank you for the supportive review. We first address your specific questions, followed by a paragraph regarding your major concern about the broader impact of finding simple interpolants.

> “... apply to CVC5?... gains specific to the algorithm behind Z3?”

There are two ways to apply our method to other solvers. One approach is to retrain the model using ground truths generated by the target solver. The other is to directly apply a model trained on ground truths from a different solver (e.g., Z3). The former is ideal, as it allows the model to learn the specific behaviors of the target solver. However, as shown in Section 4.4, even a pre-trained model can transfer effectively across solvers to some extent. In either case, **the gains are not tied to Z3's internal algorithms.** The learning framework we propose can be applied to other solvers without modification—particularly when retraining is possible.

Technically, while CVC5 supports interpolation, it struggles with our benchmark suite. In our experiments, CVC5 failed to solve 85% of the problems within the timeout of 5 seconds. For the remaining 15%, the problems were so simple that the original interpolants already had complexity 1 and could not be further simplified.

Nonetheless, we still observe significant reduction (-66%) in solver time. Below we report the statistics on guiding CVC5 using the model trained on Z3’s ground truths.

| Method | Valid | Complexity | Solver time (s)|
|:------|:-----:|:------:|:------:|
| Original CVC5 | 15.3% | 1 | 0.301 |
| Guided CVC5 | 7.3% | 1 | 0.107 |

> “What is the train and test split? ...  parallel GPU computation.”

The train-test split is 80:20, as stated on lines 220-221.  We would also like to clarify that parallel GPU computation does not introduce any form of “cheating” here. The interpolants are always computed and verified by the SMT solver which runs on CPU. The model’s role is limited to analyzing the original input formulas and providing suggestions to avoid redundancy. It does not compute the interpolants by itself using GPU power.

> “... what the broader impacts are... how we should design learning algorithms ?” & “... translate to other relevant problems in the field.”

**The main purpose of this work is to break the ice on a largely unexplored topic** — the application of learning to interpolation solving with simplification. (Please see below for its significance in verification.)  

As Reviewer eKSy noted in the review, Craig interpolation via ML has not been seriously attempted before. Consequently, there is currently no established understanding or baseline about how learning algorithms should be designed for this problem, nor what properties are desirable or generalizable.

Rather than claiming to answer the higher-level design questions, our goal is to create the first stepping stone: to show that learning-based methods can in fact produce useful results for finding simple interpolants, a symbolic reasoning task previously considered difficult to learn. The fact that our lightweight model is able to improve solvers like Z3 demonstrates that meaningful learning signals exist and can be extracted.

We believe the broader impact lies precisely here. We provide concrete empirical evidence that this new direction is feasible and promising. Future work will be better positioned to address the deeper question of how learning algorithms should be designed for interpolation and similar tasks — but such exploration must start somewhere, and we believe this paper provides a well-motivated and technically grounded beginning.

---

# Addressing the Concern on Potential Impact
We noticed that the only substantive concern raised by reviewers eKSy and gZmf centers on the potential impact of our work. Reviewer DWpJ echoed this by asking “Why is producing simpler interpolants important?”

This is an oversight on our part. While we briefly mentioned the reasons on lines 19–21, we did not elaborate further, as this fact is often taken for granted in the literature on interpolation-based verification.

We now provide a clarification on the significant impact of simpler interpolants, addressing both conceptual and practical aspects. 

We would like to emphasize that this is not an artificial problem chosen merely to showcase machine learning techniques. Rather, it addresses a longstanding and practical challenge in formal verification—one that directly impacts the effectiveness and scalability of verification tools.

## Conceptually

In program verification, Craig interpolants are often used to extract candidate invariants from proofs of bounded cases. Intuitively, an interpolant is a formula that captures a property implied by one part of the system and inconsistent with another, using only the common variables.

**The key insight is that simplicity leads to generality.** A simpler interpolant tends to omit the incidental details of a particular execution, making it more likely to hold in general (i.e. be inductive for all executions).

This is analogous to machine learning, where a simple model that captures the core pattern will generalize better than an overly complex one that overfits to training data. In the verification context, a complex interpolant can “overfit” a bounded proof (including many specific corner-case conditions), whereas a concise interpolant focuses on the essential relationship and is less prone to depend on particular aspects of that bounded run.

The result is an interpolant that is more likely to be a true invariant for the unbounded system, rather than a brittle formula that breaks with minor changes. A concise interpolant (e.g. a single linear inequality or equality) is less tied to a specific execution, so it generalizes to new executions. Invariant generation becomes easier because the formula isn’t cluttered with special-case conditions that might fail as soon as we go beyond the originally analyzed trace.

In short, simpler interpolants serve as more general and robust invariants, which is exactly what we need for scalable verification.

### **Example**:

Consider the following example of finding a loop invariant. Suppose we have a C program:
```
x = 0; y = 0;
while(*) {x++; y+=2}
assert(x=100=> y=200);
```
The key to proving the assertion lies in discovering the loop invariant y = 2x. A common strategy for finding such invariants is interpolation. 

Let $I(x,y)$ be an (unknown) invariant.

Then by unfolding the loop a few times, we would get the constraints:

$(x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4) \Rightarrow I(x,y)$

$I(x,y) \Rightarrow (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

This induces the interpolation problem:

$A = (x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4)$

$B = \neg (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

All of

$I_1 = (x=0\wedge y=0)\vee (x=1\wedge y=2)\vee (x=2 \wedge y=4)$

$I_2 = (x=100 \Rightarrow y=200)$

$I = y = 2x$

are interpolants between A and B, but only $y=2x$, the simplest among these, is a valid loop invariant of the original C program.

### **Where is the difficulty?**
In practice, interpolation solvers can (and often) generate interpolants like $I_1$ or $I_2$. In the simple two dimensional case as in this example, a human expert might be able to simplify the solutions by hand. But it quickly becomes infeasible in higher dimensions (i.e., more variables) with more regions (i.e., more logic connectives). 

Whether machine learning can guide interpolation solvers to find simpler interpolants has been an open question. Our work makes the first attempt to guide interpolation solvers toward producing simpler interpolants, and shows that this is both possible and effective.

## Practically
From an engineering perspective, using simpler interpolants pays off in the following ways.

- **Verification Convergence**: Interpolants are used iteratively to search for an inductive invariant. Simpler interpolants are more likely to generalize across all program executions, increasing the probability that one of them will be inductive. This, in turn, improves the chance that the verification process will eventually succeed. In contrast, overly complex interpolants tend to overfit bounded traces and often fail to generalize, which can cause the verification loop to stagnate or diverge entirely. As a result, the system may perform many unproductive solver calls or even time out.

- **Solver efficiency**: Less complex formulas are cheaper for solvers to handle. Every additional literal or clause in an interpolant is something the downstream SMT query has to reason about. A 447-clause interpolant might trigger many more internal computations (Boolean case splits, calls to arithmetic subsolvers, etc.) than a 2-clause interpolant. By keeping interpolants minimal, we cut down the search space and the overhead in the subsequent SAT/SMT procedures. This often translates to more solvable downstream problems and/or faster verification times, as seen in Figure 4 of [1].

- **Proof reuse**: Simpler interpolants often enable a more compositional verification approach, where one can reuse the same inductive argument across different components or unrolling lengths. If the invariant is a small conjunction of facts, it can be plugged in modularly; if it’s a huge disjunction of special cases, it’s much harder to reuse or even comprehend. Thus simplicity can improve the scalability of the verification process itself, not just the single SMT query.

For further theoretical justification and more empirical evidence, we refer to the classical literature by Aws Albarghouthi and Kenneth L. McMillan such as [1].

[1] *Beautiful Interpolants.* Aws Albarghouthi and Kenneth L. McMillan. CAV 2013: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Computer Aided Verification - Volume 8044 Pages 313 - 329

Thank you for the review. We understand that unfamiliarity with the field may have led to some confusion, and we would like to clarify each of the concerns raised.

> “Limited Evaluation: The method is evaluated on a small set of benchmark problems, with no discussion of its scalability...”

To the best of our knowledge, no benchmark suite currently exists for learning-based LIA interpolation. We presented the first dataset, and did our best to ensure complexity and a rich coverage. We detailed the complete generation process in Section 4.1 and explained how the dataset **scales** with parameters c1 and c2 in **Interp**(c1, c2).

We also respectfully disagree that our dataset consisting of 66K problems is “small” in the context of formal verification. In this field, high-quality data are much more limited than other applications of machine learning. As a reference, previous works on learning SAT typically use 8K to 10K problems. See [2] [3] for example. 

[2] *Learning a SAT Solver from Single-Bit Supervision.* D. Selsam, M. Lamm, B. Bünz, P. Liang, L. de Moura, and D. L. Dill. ICLR 2019.

[3] *Learning Better Representations From Less Data For Propositional Satisfiability.* Mohamed Ghanem and Frederik Schmitt and Julian Siber and Bernd Finkbeiner. NeurIPS 2024.

> “Lack of Comparison: The paper does not adequately compare the proposed method with other state-of-the-art techniques for simplifying interpolants ...”

As Reviewer eKSy noted, Craig interpolation via ML has not been seriously attempted before. **Direct comparisons are thus not possible—no existing method learns to simplify interpolants in LIA using neural models.**

As for the techniques on the symbolic side, our proposed approach **improves upon them**. Our approach further augments, rather than replaces, traditional symbolic methods already built into mature solvers like Z3. It learns heuristics that exploit redundancies in the input to produce simpler interpolants—something traditional approaches are not designed to do. This is why our approach is a combination of machine learning and symbolic methods. The benefits are demonstrated empirically in Section 4.

> “Interpretability: The GNN-based model's decision process is not clearly explained, which could limit its acceptance in practical, safety-critical applications.”

The GNN model does not make any decision on which disjuncts to choose. It only encodes the formulas into the latent space.

The selector model does not make any correctness-critical decisions, either. It only proposes subsets of formulas to guide interpolation. The SMT solver is ultimately responsible for computing the interpolant and guaranteeing soundness. Our approach is designed for safety-critical applications from the very beginning.

> “Theoretical Depth: The paper lacks a thorough theoretical analysis of the generalization and robustness of the model to different LIA problem structures.”

As indicated in our submission, this is an application paper (see “Primary Area” and Checklist Item 3 on theoretical guarantees). That said, we did our best to provide an analysis of the generalization and robustness of the model to different underlying solvers in Section 4.4.

However, we are unsure what is meant by “different LIA problem structures” in the question. Craig interpolation in LIA is concerned with unsatisfiable formula pairs; structural variation is implicitly captured in the disjunctive inputs we generate. If the reviewer can provide a more precise definition, we are happy to address it.

---

We hope these clarify the confusion! We would greatly appreciate it if you could take our response into account when considering the final score.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a novel learning-based approach to improve interpolation solvers for Linear Integer Arithmetic (LIA) by generating simpler interpolants. The authors propose using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) combined with a self-attention mechanism to learn embeddings of LIA formulas, which capture both local arithmetic constraints and the global structure of the formulas. These embeddings enable the model to identify the most relevant subsets of the formulas to create minimal, valid interpolants, thereby simplifying the interpolation process.

The method is integrated with existing SMT solvers like Z3, showing significant improvements in performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach achieves up to 47.3% reduction in interpolant complexity for modern solvers and up to 69.1% reduction for older solvers, offering a promising solution for software and hardware verification. The authors argue that this approach combines symbolic reasoning with machine learning, making it a practical and efficient enhancement for formal verification tasks.

summary.value:
At a high level, this paper proposes a novel graph-neural-network-based approach for learning how to allocate attention when focusing on relationships between formulas when doing Craig interpolation for Linear Integer Arithmetic (LIA). When solving verification problems, verifiers are often producing Craig interpolants in a tight loop alongside enumeration. Thus, these Craig interpolants can be thought of as "intermediate formulas" which the solver (verifier, etc.) is exploring on its way to a solution (counterexample, proof, etc.). In the case of LIA, these look like polynomial (in)equalities. Traditional approaches to Craig interpolation produce unwieldy, large interpolants, with possibly-large coefficients--incurring unnecessarily-large state-space enumeration in the subsequent saturation part of the engine / verifier. The goal is to get small (but correct) interpolants.

The authors approach is to deeply integrate a GNN and a self-attention-based selector mechanism. The GNN encodes semantic relationships between clauses in the knowledge base, and a selector network then selects subsets of formulas from which to attempt to generate interpolants. This requires a new dataset of interpolation problems--the authors build a new dataset of 66k LIA interpolation problems, which seems like a seriously hefty dataset to me.

The authors emphasize the needs to focus on traditional ML and a GNN-based approach, and that it would be especially irrelevant to use an LLM. I agree, it would be irrelevant to use an LLM here. The authors also stress the importance of calling the solver *once*, rather than in a loop, in a bottom-up fashion. This necessitates that the authors decompose their exploration in a top-down manner. 

# Overall score and justification

Overall, I am very impressed by this work. However, I am very surprised that this is not a very hot area, and it seems surprising to me that Craig interpolation via ML has not been seriously attempted before. My main concern rests on the significance of the work. The authors show reduced interpolant complexity, but I have an outstanding question: how can I put this work into perspective in terms of its impact on the field? Even though small interpolants are nice, are they really a critical component in verification pipelines?

I cannot tell if this paper is a cool, incremental contribution to a challenging field or a truly revolutionary step forward. However, in either case it is well written, intuitive, and easy to read, even as an outsider. I argue that it should be accepted.

Some caveats about my review: I am knowledgable about Craig interpolation and its use in verification, but I do not deeply understand the mechanisms for constructing Craig interpolants and am not sure I am fully prepared to give a nuanced review versus the state of the art.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths 

- Craig interpolation is an important, long-standing, challenging problem that sits at the tight loop of verification, SMT solving, and many important problems in logic and automated reasoning. This paper attacks a particularly pertinent instance of Craig interpolation: for LIA, an important first-order theory that is one of the most popular in SMTLIB.

- The authors got real interpolation problems from downstream tasks, though it is a bit unclear exactly what these are. The authors build a huge knowledge database of LIA facts and then compute self-attention between all of them, which would appear to be a very compelling approach, to me. It is really using the self-attention idea in a manner that can credibly inform the construction of interpolants in an on-demand way.

- The encodings of formulas (Sec 3.2) is brief but makes a lot of sense. You want to be able to learn the hierarchical structure of formulas. Naturally, you need to run as many rounds of iteration as the tallest AST you have (one would assume).

- Writing is overall of high caliber and makes sense. 

# Weaknesses

- The major weakness is limited potential impact. It seems that there is limited downstream application for making small Craig interpolants. At least, the authors have included no compelling evaluation which demonstrates why we should believe this will be the case. This is a potentially major concern, although I do believe the approach is still relevant and interesting nonetheless.

- The idea of pooling together all interpolants seen dynamically throughout tons of sample instances seems reasonable, but importantly seems to throw away the context inherent to the problem. I am not sure if this is a weakness or if this is explicitly something you want to do.

questions.value:
- There is a depth into the tree, but not any structural information. How is this depth used? I guess the hierarchical information is captured by the MPNN?

- How do I put your approach into context for how this might impact the future of SMT solvers and verification? I understand in the abstract that small interpolants are good--but no experiments in the paper can convince me of the promise of the approach to, say, accelerate SMT. Do you have any thoughts on this?

final_justification.value:
I argue the paper should be accepted. The authors have offered convincing, thoughtful, and reflective commentary and feedback, both in the original paper and in the subsequent rebuttal.

The paper is on a complex, challenging, and important area--complaints that the paper needs to be changed to accommodate non-experts are unfounded, as the paper tackles a well-known, important, and long-standing problem. The authors provide further detail in their rebuttal here--I would encourage them to incorporate some of this feedback into the paper, anticipating that it might help the paper's context with respect to work appearing at NeurIPS.

The authors offer convincing evidence that their approach is promising, at least good enough over the existing state of the art that it is worthy of publication at NeurIPS '25.

The scoping of paper, size of contribution, and evaluation of results is reasonable, even for a top conference.

Here is my only negative feedback to the authors: what you wrote above, and to a degree in the paper, is a thoughtful argument that makes a lot of intuitive sense--as someone who is somewhat-versed in the usage of Craig interpolation, the reasoning above makes total sense to me. Ideally, work appearing at NeurIPS (or any other top conference) would also take the reasoning above and truly demonstrate the impact on downstream tasks--that is a bit lacking in this paper. However, I do not see that alone as a reason for rejecting this paper--I do not want to see that happen, in this case, and feel it is unfair to impose that standard given all of the work the authors have done here.

I argue the paper should be accepted, and maintain my score. I encourage the AC to consider the importance, relevance, generality, and long-standing nature of the problem being attacked in this work.

My score is 5--I recognize the paper has some flaws, but (with no intended offense to other reviewers) I think it is important to argue for strong, technically-focused work with rich technical foundations. The paper harmonizes machine learning with a challenging and relevant task that lies at the core of automated reasoning.

I do not argue 6 because I recognize that the paper does have some attack surface, but I think given the totality of the situation, it would be best for NeurIPS '25 to accept the paper.

summary.value:
Linear integer arithmetic (LIA), is a logic that allows one to express linear
constraints on integers: equalities, inequalities, and divisibility by non-zero integers. 
This paper proposes a learning-based approach toward computing simpler (than previous logic based
methods) interpolants in LIA, complementing. In addition, they provide a new large dataset of interpolation problems
on which they demonstrate the  ability of their learning approach to simplify interpolants compared to previous approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
1. The problem of computing interpolants for ILA is useful for program verification.
2. The paper uses light weight learning rather than LLMs
3. The Dataset provided could be certainly  useful for testing solutions for this problem in the future.

Weaknesses
1. Its unclear to what extent one can verify the claim of "simplicity" compared to previous solutions, the definition
of simplicity was not made clear.
2. Quoting "We show that when Z3 is guided by our learned model, the complexity of the interpolants it produces can
be reduced by up to 47.3%". Not sure how this figure was reached. Also, does this mean that the simpler interpolants were more useful?

questions.value:
I am not an expert in the field.
It would help me to understand exactly where and how interpolants are used and why the 
problem of producing "simpler" interpolants is important as well as a better explanation of the 
"simplicity" definition.

title.value: Learning Simple Interpolants for Linear Integer Arithmetic

abstract.value: Craig interpolation plays a central role in formal verification tasks such as model checking, invariant generation, and abstraction refinement. In the domain of linear integer arithmetic (LIA), interpolants are crucial for deriving inductive invariants that characterize unreachable or safe program states, enabling scalable and precise reasoning about software and hardware correctness. Despite progress in interpolation algorithms, generating concise and interpretable interpolants remains a key challenge. We propose a lightweight learning-based approach to generating simple interpolants for LIA. Our model learns to lazily sample input problems directly and is complementary to existing logical methods. When Z3 is guided by our learned model, the complexity of the interpolants it produces can be reduced by up to 47.3%. For older solvers, the reduction rate can reach up to 69.1%.
